'''Peter Vincent Douglas''' (born November 23, 1955) is an American television and film producer. He is the third son of actor [[Kirk Douglas]], and the first by his second wife, German-American producer [[Anne Buydens]].<ref name="bio">[http://www.vincentpictures.com/who-we-are/peter-douglas Biography]</ref> Douglas worked closely with his father and became president of [[The Bryna Company]], an independent film and television production company formed by Kirk Douglas in 1949. In 1978, he formed his own film production company, Vincent Pictures.<ref>{{Cite web|title=VINCENT PICTURES :: California (US) :: OpenCorporates|url=https://opencorporates.com/companies/us_ca/C0871069|access-date=2021-06-15|website=opencorporates.com}}</ref>

Douglas won a [[Primetime Emmy Awards|Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama/Comedy Special]] in 1988 for his production of ''[[Inherit the Wind (1988 film)|Inherit the Wind]]'', which co-starred his father and [[Jason Robards]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Peter Douglas|url=http://www.imdb.com/name/nm0235209/awards|access-date=2021-06-19|website=IMDb}}</ref> He had been nominated for the same award two years prior for his production of ''[[Amos (film)|Amos]]'', which also starred his father.<ref name=":1" />

==Life and career==
Peter Douglas was born in Los Angeles, California, on November 23, 1955.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Variety|url=https://archive.org/details/variety200-1955-11|title=Variety (November 1955)|date=1955|publisher=New York, NY: Variety Publishing Company|others=Media History Digital Library}}</ref> His middle name was given in homage to [[Vincent van Gogh]], whom his father was portraying in a film version being shot in Europe at the time of his birth.<ref name=":0" /> The film in question, ''[[Lust for Life (1956 film)|Lust for Life]]'', was later released in 1956. In 1958, his father named his new [[Music publisher|music publishing]] company, [[Peter Vincent Music|Peter Vincent Music Corporation]] (a subsidiary of [[Bryna Productions]]), after his son,<ref name=":04">{{Cite web|title=Archival Resources in Wisconsin: Descriptive Finding Aids|url=https://digicoll.library.wisc.edu/cgi/f/findaid/findaid-idx?c=wiarchives;cc=wiarchives;view=text;rgn=main;didno=uw-whs-us0102an|access-date=2021-05-24|website=digicoll.library.wisc.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/cashbox23unse_46|title=Cash Box|date=1962-08-11|publisher=Cash Box Pub. Co.|others=William and Mary Libraries Special Collections Research Center}}</ref> while Peter later named his own independent film production company Vincent Pictures.<ref name="bio" /> In 1958, a young Peter was seen on the television program ''[[This Is Your Life (American franchise)|This Is Your Life]]'', which was honoring the life and career of his father.<ref>{{Citation|title=Kirk Douglas|date=1958-05-28|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0721400/?ref_=nm_flmg_slf_7|type=Biography, Family, Reality-TV|others=Anne Douglas, Joel Douglas, Kirk Douglas, Michael Douglas|access-date=2021-06-19}}</ref>

Douglas' early work in the film industry was tied to his father, namely through his independent film production company, Bryna Productions. As a child, Douglas had uncredited bit parts in his father's films ''[[The Vikings (film)|The Vikings]]'' and ''[[Strangers When We Meet (film)|Stranger When We Meet]]'' (in which Kirk Douglas both starred and produced).<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Montgomery Advertiser from Montgomery, Alabama on May 6, 1960 · 44|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/256038804/|access-date=2021-05-25|website=Newspapers.com|date=May 6, 1960 |language=en}}</ref> Douglas went to high school at a military academy in Southern California.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=Dayton Daily News from Dayton, Ohio on August 16, 1980 · 34|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/405935753/|access-date=2021-06-15|website=Newspapers.com|date=August 16, 1980 |language=en}}</ref>

In the early 1970s, Douglas studied photography at the Los Angeles Art Center.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Philadelphia Inquirer from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on August 17, 1980 · Page 170|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/171521282/|access-date=2021-06-20|website=Newspapers.com|date=August 17, 1980 |language=en}}</ref> In June 1972, aged 17, Douglas was hired by his father as the [[still photographer]] when The Bryna Company produced ''[[Scalawag (film)|Scalawag]]'' on location in [[Yugoslavia]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Orlando Sentinel from Orlando, Florida on August 7, 1972 · Page 42|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/225061339/|access-date=2021-06-05|website=Newspapers.com|date=August 7, 1972 |language=en}}</ref> His father produced, directed, and starred in the film, while his mother, Anne, was co-producer; his younger brother, Eric, was the producer's assistant, and their family dog, Shaft, had a part in the film.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Gazette from Cedar Rapids, Iowa on September 26, 1973 · 39|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/550180814/|access-date=2021-06-16|website=Newspapers.com|date=September 26, 1973 |language=en}}</ref> During the production of ''Scalawag'', actress [[Lesley-Anne Down]] posed nude for Peter and the pictures were sold to ''[[Playboy]]'' magazine.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Post-Standard from Syracuse, New York on October 4, 1972 · Page 41|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/36544079/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Newspapers.com|date=October 4, 1972 |language=en}}</ref> Douglas again served as still photographer when his family traveled from Yugoslavia to England for The Bryna Company's television musical film ''Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde''. Pictures taken by Douglas of the character's transformation were used on the cover of ''[[Los Angeles Times]]''<nowiki/>' ''TV Times'' section on March 4, 1973.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Los Angeles Times from Los Angeles, California on March 4, 1973 · 442|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/382704176/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Newspapers.com|date=March 4, 1973 |language=en}}</ref>

Douglas attended the [[University of California at Santa Barbara]] for a year and a half but ultimately dropped out to focus on photography and motion picture work.<ref name=":3" /> In November 1973, Douglas photographed his brother Michael and his at-the-time girlfriend [[Brenda Vaccaro]] in their [[Benedict Canyon, Los Angeles|Benedict Canyon]] home for publication in several leading magazines.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Intelligencer Journal from Lancaster, Pennsylvania on November 23, 1973 · 29|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/559442237/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Newspapers.com|date=November 23, 1973 |language=en}}</ref> He also became Olympic swimmer [[Mark Spitz]]'s official photographer.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=The Philadelphia Inquirer from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on August 17, 1980 · Page 170|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/171521282/|access-date=2021-06-20|website=Newspapers.com|date=August 17, 1980 |language=en}}</ref> In March 1974, Douglas formed his own photographic service company and photography studio, Bryna International, and was represented by talent agent Phyllis Carlyle through her agency A-Plus.'''<ref>{{Cite web|title=Chicago Tribune from Chicago, Illinois on March 14, 1974 · 42|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/383976115/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Newspapers.com|date=March 14, 1974 |language=en}}</ref>''' Carlyle landed Douglas photography contracts for such publications as ''[[Cosmopolitan (magazine)|Cosmopolitan]]'' and large advertisement agencies.<ref name=":2" /> In June 1974, Douglas photographed [[Frank Sinatra]] cooking a special Italian dinner for his parents' anniversary and the pictures were used in several publications.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Pittsburgh Press from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on June 9, 1974 · Page 306|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/147334088/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Newspapers.com|date=June 9, 1974 |language=en}}</ref>

For The Bryna Company's next picture, ''[[Posse (1975 film)|Posse]]'', filmed from September to November 1974, Douglas served as post-production supervisor.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Fort Worth Star-Telegram from Fort Worth, Texas on May 22, 1975 · 16|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/637278643/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=Newspapers.com|date=May 22, 1975 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Yumpu.com|title=Boxoffice-December.09.1974|url=https://www.yumpu.com/en/document/read/31903271/boxoffice-december091974|access-date=2021-06-14|website=yumpu.com|language=en}}</ref> Douglas then began working on the development of [[Ray Bradbury]]'s ''[[Something Wicked This Way Comes (film)|Something Wicked This Way Comes]]'', which would take nine years to complete and was eventually filmed as a coproduction between The Bryna Company and [[Walt Disney Productions]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Los Angeles Times from Los Angeles, California on August 15, 1976 · 206|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/383028336/|access-date=2021-06-18|website=Newspapers.com|date=August 15, 1976 |language=en}}</ref> Douglas also worked as a producer's assistant at Columbia Pictures during the mid-to-late 1970s.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Evening Sun from Baltimore, Maryland on July 25, 1980 · 29|url=http://www.newspapers.com/newspage/371841033/|access-date=2021-06-20|website=Newspapers.com|date=July 25, 1980 |language=en}}</ref>

Peter Douglas' television production credits include ''[[Inherit the Wind (1988 film)|Inherit the Wind]]'' (1988), for which he won the Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama or Comedy Special, and ''Amos'' (1984), which was also Emmy-nominated in the same category. His motion picture credits include the science-fiction time-travel classic ''[[The Final Countdown (film)|The Final Countdown]]'' (1980), in which his father starred, and the adaptation of the classic Ray Bradbury novel ''[[Something Wicked This Way Comes (film)|Something Wicked This Way Comes]]'' (1983), which won the Saturn Award for Best Fantasy Film. He also produced the suspense-comedy hit ''[[Fletch (film)|Fletch]]'' (1985), as well as its sequel ''[[Fletch Lives]]'' (1989), both starring [[Chevy Chase]].<ref name="bio" /> In December 1985, it was reported that Peter Douglas and [[Michael Phillips (producer)|Michael Phillips]] were working on developing a film from [[Isaac Asimov]]'s novel ''[[The End of Eternity]]'' for [[TriStar Pictures|Tri-Star Pictures]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_variety_1985-12-25_321_9|title=Variety 1985-12-25: Vol 321 Iss 9|date=1985-12-25|language=English}}</ref> The property would remain in development for several years but was never filmed.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_variety_1991-02-25_342_7_0|title=Variety 1991-02-25: Vol 342 Iss 7|date=1991-02-25|language=English}}</ref>

Douglas wrote, directed, and produced the independent film ''[[A Tiger's Tale]]'' (1988), starring [[Ann-Margret]]. He was the executive producer of the HBO Drama thriller ''[[The Enemy Within (1994 film)|The Enemy Within]]'', starring [[Forest Whitaker]] and [[Jason Robards]], and was also executive producer of the 2009 motion picture ''[[Whip It (film)|Whip It]]'' starring [[Drew Barrymore]] and [[Elliot Page]].<ref name="bio" />

Douglas married Lisa Schroeder in 1991. They have four children.<ref name="bio" />

In 2012, Vincent Pictures announced that Peter Douglas was working on a remake of the 1966 film ''[[Grand Prix (1966 film)|Grand Prix]]'', which his father executive produced through [[Douglas and Lewis Productions]].<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_variety_march-12-18-2012_426_5|title=Variety March 12-18, 2012: Vol 426 Iss 5|date=2012-03-12|language=English}}</ref>
